item.title: Planning a Course with AI: From Learning Goals to a First-Draft Syllabus
item.description:
Part 3 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.

Course planning is where AI earns its keep for most faculty. It is also where its mistakes are easiest to miss. In the California State University system’s fall 2025 survey, developing course materials was the most common way faculty used AI, at 55%. This post gives a routine that works in any discipline, whether you teach organic chemistry, first-year writing or a studio course. It follows the familiar “backward design” order:

  1. Decide what students should be able to do.
  2. Decide how you will know they can do it.
  3. Plan the weeks.

AI drafts each step; you decide.

Step 1: Set up a course workspace (15 minutes, once)

Most licensed AI tools now let you save instructions and files in one place, so you don’t start from scratch each time. Depending on what your college offers, that place might be a NotebookLM notebook, a Gemini Gem, a ChatGPT project or custom GPT, a Claude project or a Copilot notebook.

Create one for the course and add:

  • the catalog description and any department or general-education outcomes the course must meet;
  • your last syllabus and schedule, if you have taught it before;
  • your own notes on what worked and what did not;
  • openly licensed or library-provided readings you already plan to use.

Do not add student work, grades or student comments (see Part 2).

Then paste in standing instructions, so every request follows the same rules:

You are helping me plan [COURSE NAME], a [level, e.g., 200-level] course in [discipline]
for [who takes it, e.g., sophomores, mostly non-majors] at a small liberal arts college.
Work only from the files I provided and what I tell you. Never invent readings, citations,
page numbers, dates or college policies. When you need one, write [READING NEEDED],
[DATE NEEDED] or [POLICY NEEDED] instead. Keep suggestions realistic for a class of
[number] students meeting [days and length]. Ask me a question if something is unclear.

Step 2: Draft learning goals (15 minutes)

Draft 5 to 7 learning outcomes for this course. Each must start with an observable verb
(analyze, design, compare, explain, create...), fit the catalog description, and be
something a student could show in [the number of weeks] weeks. For each outcome, add one
sentence on how a student would demonstrate it. Mark which outcomes cover the department
or general-education outcomes in my files.

Read the list against your own sense of the course. Expect to rewrite. The value is a structured starting point and options you might not have considered, not a finished answer. Cut anything that sounds generic, such as “develop critical thinking skills”, unless you can say exactly how students will show it.

Step 3: Align assignments to the goals (20 minutes)

For the outcomes I approved (pasted below), propose a set of assessments for the semester.
For each, give: which outcomes it measures, format, approximate student hours, and when in
the term it fits. Include at least one assessment that students complete in class or
explain orally, so it shows their own understanding. Finish with a table: rows = outcomes,
columns = assessments, cells = how strongly each assessment measures each outcome.

That last table, an alignment map, is the most useful thing in this step. It shows outcomes that nothing measures and assignments that measure nothing you care about. Check the student-hours column against your college’s credit-hour expectations. AI is often optimistic about how long things take.

Step 4: Map the weeks, but do the dates yourself

AI tools are unreliable at calendar arithmetic, such as which weekday a holiday falls on or how many class meetings fit before break. So build the calendar first:

  1. Open your college’s academic calendar.
  2. Type every class meeting date into a simple table in a document or spreadsheet, and mark holidays and breaks.

Then ask AI only to fill topics into the rows you made:

Here is my table of class meetings (dates already filled in; do not change them).
Fill in the Topic and Preparation columns so the course builds toward the assessments
in the order I approved. Keep one main topic per meeting. Put [READING NEEDED] wherever
a reading should go. Leave the rows marked BREAK empty.

Step 5: Find readings yourself

Never accept a citation an AI suggests without finding the source yourself. In a 2025 study, GPT-4o fabricated almost 1 in 5 of the references it produced, and fabrication was worse on specialized topics, which is exactly where faculty need help. Ask instead for search terms and the kinds of sources to look for:

For each [READING NEEDED] slot, suggest 3 search phrases I could use in our library
databases and the type of source that would fit (primary source, review article,
textbook chapter, case study, dataset). Do not name specific titles or authors.

Then search your library’s databases or ask your subject librarian. Only list what you have actually opened.

Step 6: Write the policies in your own voice

AI can draft standard syllabus sections such as attendance, late work and accessibility. Start from your college’s required syllabus language. Your AI-use policy for students is worth writing yourself, because it signals what you value. A useful structure:

  1. Where AI is welcome.
  2. Where it is not.
  3. How students should disclose AI use.
  4. What happens if they don’t.

Step 7: Keep it yours

According to the US Copyright Office, prompts alone don’t make you the author of what AI generates, but your selection, arrangement and revision can be protected. Beyond copyright, the course should sound like you. Keep a short “changes” note as you edit: what you cut, rewrote or added. That note also becomes your starting point next year.

Next year: revise from evidence

At the end of the term, add to the workspace:

  • your “changes” note;
  • your reflections;
  • aggregate results only, such as which quiz questions most students missed, or the three most common themes in course evaluations, with no names and no quotes from small classes.

Then ask:

Using my notes and these aggregate results, suggest the three revisions most likely to
improve student learning next term. For each, say which outcome it serves, what evidence
in my files supports it, and what it would cost me in preparation time.

Try it this week

  1. Pick a course you will teach next term.
  2. Do Steps 1 to 3. Plan on about 50 minutes.
  3. Compare the alignment map with your current syllabus. Find one outcome that nothing measures well, or one assignment that doesn’t map to any outcome.
  4. Write down the minutes it took, and whether the result was better than what you would have done alone.

Next time: making quizzes, handouts and slides with AI, and catching the specific mistakes AI tends to make.

Have a planning prompt that works well in your discipline? Send it to me at lip AT etown DOT edu, and I may include it in a later post.

Sources

  • Inside Higher Ed, California State University faculty AI survey (fall 2025)
  • UConn eCampus, Backward design with AI
  • JMIR, Citation fabrication by GPT-4o (2025)
  • US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability (2025)

item.title: Before You Paste: Student Privacy and Choosing the Right AI Tool
item.description:
Part 2 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.

It is 11 p.m., you have 30 essays left, and a free chatbot is one tab away. Pasting in a student’s essay to “get started on feedback” feels harmless. It may not be. Before any of the later posts in this series, it is worth spending ten minutes on what you may put into which tool.

This post is general guidance, not legal advice. Your college’s policies and counsel have the final word.

FERPA in plain words

FERPA, the federal student-privacy law, covers education records: grades, submitted work, advising notes, accommodation information and emails about a student, among others. You can see your own students’ records because you have a legitimate educational interest in them. Sharing those records with an outside company is different.

An outside service may receive education records without each student’s consent only if the college treats it as a “school official”. That means it performs a service the college would otherwise do itself, is under the college’s direct control over how the records are used and kept, and may not pass them on. In practice, that takes a contract.

Two misunderstandings are common:

  • “The company promises not to train on my data." A no-training promise is helpful, but on its own it is not the same as the college’s control over use, retention and deletion. Free personal accounts do not give the college that control.
  • “I removed the student’s name, so it’s anonymous." At a small college, often not. A course list, a project topic or a detail like “the only veteran in the class” can identify a student. Removing names is good practice. Do it, but don’t treat the result as anonymous.

The traffic-light rule

Most colleges already classify their data. Map those classes to AI tools like this, and post the table where you will see it.

Kind of information Examples Personal AI accounts College-licensed AI (under contract) College-hosted private AI
Green: public Catalog, published syllabi, public web pages, published papers Yes Yes Yes
Yellow: internal Draft committee reports, internal procedures No Yes Yes
Orange: confidential or student records Grades, student work, advising notes, personnel files, search materials No Only if your college approves that tool for this kind of data Only if your college approves it for this kind of data
Red: highly restricted Social Security numbers, financial-aid tax data, health and disability records, passwords No No No

Two rules sit on top of the table:

  • Never record tenure, promotion, grievance or conduct deliberations, whatever tool you use.
  • Don’t ask an unapproved tool to “remove the names” from identifiable text. By the time it removes them, it has already received them.

Which tools you probably already have

Most colleges already pay for at least one education-tier AI tool, often without announcing it:

  • Google campuses: the Gemini app and NotebookLM are “core services” in Google Workspace for Education, turned on by default for higher education since 2025. Google states that this data is not reviewed by humans or used to train its models.
  • Microsoft campuses: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat with enterprise data protection comes with the standard education licenses. The full Microsoft 365 Copilot is a paid add-on.
  • Contracted tools: ChatGPT Edu and Claude for Education are sold to institutions under contract. Whether student records may go into them depends on that contract.
  • College-hosted: some colleges run their own AI on campus servers. My college’s EMTutor pilot is one example. Data stays on campus, but the college is responsible for securing it.

Universities read the same product differently. One major university allows student records in ChatGPT Edu under its contract, while another advises against uploading academic records even with a license. Another found a data-sharing setting turned on by default in its workspace. So the only list that matters is your own college’s.

Try it this week

  1. Find your college’s approved-tools list. Search your IT or teaching-center website for “AI tools” or “approved software”. If there is no list, email IT one question: “Which AI tools are approved for FERPA-protected student information, and which only for public or internal information?" Until you hear back, treat everything except green as not allowed in AI tools.
  2. Sign in the protected way. Use the AI tool through your college account, not a personal one. In Copilot, look for the indicator that enterprise data protection is on. In Gemini or NotebookLM, check that the account in the corner is your college account.
  3. Fix your personal account settings. If you also use a personal ChatGPT account for public material, open Settings → Data controls and turn off “Improve the model for everyone”.
  4. Clean up. Look through your past chats in any personal AI account. Delete any that contain student work, grades or names.
  5. Practice de-identifying. Before pasting anything about students into an approved tool:
    • Remove names, ID numbers and email addresses.
    • Remove details that identify someone by context.
    • Summarize groups instead of individuals.
    • Don’t report on groups of fewer than five students.

For chairs and directors: a one-page policy

If your department or office has no AI policy yet, one page is enough to cover:

  • Approved tools. Which tools may be used with which kind of data (link the table above).
  • Responsibility. Whoever uses AI is responsible for the accuracy of what they submit.
  • Decisions. AI makes no final decisions on grades, admissions, hiring, discipline or financial aid.
  • Disclosure. AI use is disclosed where an outside body requires it.
  • Recording. Meetings are recorded only with consent, and sensitive deliberations never.
  • Incidents. Problems are reported to IT promptly.
  • Review. The policy is reviewed once a year.

Next time, with the rules settled, we start on the fun part: planning a course with AI, from learning goals to a first-draft syllabus.

Questions about your own situation? Write to me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • FERPA regulations, 34 CFR 99.31 (the “school official” and de-identification provisions)
  • US Department of Education Privacy Technical Assistance Center, Protecting student privacy while using online educational services
  • Future of Privacy Forum and Center for Democracy & Technology guidance on vendor contracts (FPF, CDT)
  • Google, Gemini and NotebookLM as core services for education and data protection
  • Microsoft, Copilot in education
  • Examples of differing university guidance: Carnegie Mellon, BYU, University of Illinois
  • Virginia Tech, Responsible use of AI in advising

item.title: Let AI Draft, You Decide: Where AI Actually Saves Faculty and Staff Time
item.description:
Part 1 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.

Ask colleagues whether AI saves them time, and the answers split. Some say it has given them back an evening a week. Others say it has added work: checking what it wrote, rewriting what it got wrong, and worrying about students who use it. Both groups are right, and the research explains why.

This series is for faculty and staff in every discipline, not just computer science. Over the next three weeks, I will cover one area per post: protecting student data, planning courses, making materials, giving feedback, tutoring, advising, scheduling and committee work. Every post ends with steps you can try that week with tools your college probably already has.

AI use is now normal, but time savings are not

AI use among faculty grew quickly. In Tyton Partners’ national surveys, the share of instructors using generative AI at least weekly rose from 30% in 2025 to 52% in 2026. In the California State University system’s fall 2025 survey of more than 6,000 faculty, 55% said they use AI to develop course materials.

Time savings are a different story. Among instructors who use AI every day, 36% report a lighter workload, 39% report no change and 26% report a heavier one. Much of the extra work comes from dealing with students’ AI use. So far, no controlled study has measured how many hours faculty save on syllabi, slides or quizzes compared with doing the work by hand.

The studies that do measure time point to a pattern:

  • Repeatable tasks with a clear structure get faster. In one study, instructors took about 27 minutes to analyze their own course-evaluation comments. ChatGPT runs took 10 to 15 minutes.
  • Open-ended “help me with this” use can be slower. In a randomized study at a 2025 computing-education conference, teaching assistants who started from AI-drafted feedback took longer than those who wrote their own, and some let the AI’s mistakes through.

Gains go to people who build a repeatable routine, not to people who simply have access.

The rule: let AI draft, you decide

Across all the research I reviewed, one rule kept appearing. AI is good at producing first drafts: rewording, summarizing, organizing, generating options and explaining. It is unreliable at anything with a right answer that it cannot check:

  • Facts and requirements it was not given, such as a course prerequisite or a college policy
  • Dates, such as which weekday a holiday falls on
  • Citations: in one 2025 study, GPT-4o made up almost 1 in 5 of the references it produced
  • Judgments about people, such as grades, advising decisions and hiring

So divide the work. Let AI draft. Then let something you trust decide: the official catalog, your calendar, your rubric, a test, a colleague, your own expertise.

Three habits that make AI worth the time

1. Give it your material, not its memory. Upload your syllabus, the catalog or the reading, and tell it to work only from that. Then ask it to quote the sentence that supports each claim. That one instruction turns hidden guesses into things you can check in seconds.

2. One task per request. Ask for one learning goal, one quiz question or one paragraph at a time. In a 2025 study of AI-generated programming exercises, tasks covered every requested concept 94% of the time when they targeted one concept, but only 40% of the time when they targeted three. Small requests are easier to get right and easier to check.

3. Check it like a reviewer, and time yourself. Read every draft the way you would read a new colleague’s work: assume it is mostly right and look for the specific error. Write down how many minutes the task took. If AI makes a task slower or less accurate, stop using it for that task. That is a good result, not a failure.

Why this matters more at a small college

Small colleges use AI about as much as large universities, but have far fewer people to support it. Nationally, only about 1 in 10 chief academic officers report a central AI strategy at their institution, and only 6% of faculty fully agree that their institution gives them enough training. At a small college, a few people’s time is the scarce resource. A short, shared playbook is worth more than another tool license.

The series

Part Date Topic
1 Nov 23 Let AI draft, you decide (this post)
2 Nov 25 Before you paste: student privacy and choosing the right AI tool
3 Nov 27 Planning a course with AI: from learning goals to a draft syllabus
4 Nov 29 Course materials you can trust: quizzes, handouts, slides and accessibility
5 Dec 1 Feedback and grading: where AI helps and where it slows you down
6 Dec 3 A tutor for every student, without giving away answers or privacy
7 Dec 5 AI for faculty advisors: meeting prep without risking student records
8 Dec 7 For chairs: course offerings, teaching loads and schedules
9 Dec 9 Committee work, accreditation, and measuring the time you save

Try it this week

  1. Pick one task you do every week, such as writing a course announcement, summarizing a reading for discussion or drafting review questions. Choose something that uses no student information.
  2. Time yourself doing it the usual way once, and write down the minutes.
  3. Do it again with AI, using your college’s licensed tool (Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, ChatGPT Edu or Claude, signed in with your college account) and this prompt:
I will paste [my lecture notes / the reading / last week's announcement].
Using ONLY this material, draft [a 150-word announcement / five discussion questions / a one-paragraph summary].
After the draft, list each factual claim you made and quote the sentence from my material that supports it.
If a claim is not supported by my material, mark it [CHECK].
  1. Check the [CHECK] items, edit the draft and time the whole process, including your checking.
  2. Compare the two times. Keep the routine only if it was faster and at least as good.

Next time: what you may and may not paste into an AI tool, and how to find out which tools your college has approved.

Questions or examples from your own discipline? Write to me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • Tyton Partners, Time for Class 2025 and the 2026 report release
  • Inside Higher Ed, California State University faculty AI survey (fall 2025)
  • eCampus News, Faculty workload can drop with daily AI use (2025)
  • BMC Medical Education, AI analysis of course-evaluation comments (2024)
  • Ahmed et al., Augmenting teaching assistants with AI for programming feedback, SIGCSE 2025
  • Jacobs et al., Generating programming tasks with multiple concepts (2025)
  • JMIR, Citation fabrication by GPT-4o (2025)
  • Inside Higher Ed, 2026 survey of chief academic officers
  • Digital Education Council, Global AI Faculty Survey 2025
  • EDUCAUSE, The digital AI divide between institutions (2025)

item.title: Coding Agents in the Small-College CS Classroom
item.description:
A year ago, the question in CS department hallways was whether students should be allowed to use ChatGPT on homework. That question is already out of date. Tools like Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex are not chatbots that hand you a snippet. They are agents: they read a whole project, edit files, run the tests, see what broke and try again. Brown University’s new intro course design puts the difference well. A chat tool produces code “without an underlying validation and revision loop”; an agent has that loop built in.

For a typical assignment in an intro or mid-level course, an agent can produce working code in minutes. So the question for those of us who teach computing is no longer whether students will use these tools. It is what a computer science education should build when typing code is no longer the hard part.

I teach computer science at Elizabethtown College, a small liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, and I run an undergraduate research lab. Below is my reading of the evidence so far, and why I think small colleges are in an unusually good position to get this right.

What the evidence says so far

The research is young, but a consistent picture is forming.

AI widens the gap between students. In “The Widening Gap,” Prather and colleagues watched novices solve a programming problem with generative AI tools across 21 lab sessions, using interviews and eye tracking. Students who were already doing well used the tools to speed up code they had planned to write anyway. Students who struggled found their existing difficulties compounded. Many thought they had done better than they had, and “finished with an illusion of competence.”

Handing off the work can cost the learning. In a randomized trial Anthropic published in January 2026, 52 mostly junior engineers learned an unfamiliar Python library, with or without AI help. The AI group averaged about 50% on the follow-up quiz, against 67% for those who coded by hand, and it was not significantly faster. The biggest gap was on debugging questions. How people used the AI mattered, though: participants who asked conceptual follow-up questions retained far more than those who let the AI write or fix the code for them.

Feeling faster is not the same as being faster. In METR’s 2025 randomized study, experienced open-source developers working in their own large codebases took about 19% longer when they could use early-2025 AI tools. Afterward, they still believed the tools had sped them up by about 20%. If seasoned professionals misjudge their own productivity that badly, we should not expect students to judge their own learning accurately.

The entry-level job market is shifting. Using ADP payroll data, Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen at Stanford found a 13% relative decline in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations. Early-career software developers were among the hardest hit, and the declines were concentrated where AI automates work rather than assisting with it. Their monthly dashboard still shows the pattern. Our graduates will be competing for jobs where “I can write the code” is no longer enough.

Educators have not figured it out either. An ACM task force surveyed 763 computing educators from 49 countries in 2025. Their top concern was students’ growing dependency on the technology (87%). Of those who answered the question, 68% had already changed how they assess students. The most common barrier to adapting was a lack of examples of best practices (48%). Nobody has a playbook yet, so small programs can experiment without waiting for one.

Why a small college is well placed

Most of the published experiments come from large universities. Yet nearly every promising idea in them depends on something small colleges already do well.

Small classes make oral assessment practical. The most direct response to AI-written code is to ask students to explain it. Researchers at Utah State made a 15-minute code review interview mandatory after every weekly assignment in a 96-student CS1 course. Students could use AI as much as they liked, as long as they could justify their code in the interview. Running it took eleven trained teaching assistants. At a college where classes are small, the professor can hold many of those conversations in person. We also know our students well enough to notice when a student’s confidence has drifted away from their understanding, which is exactly the illusion of competence the research describes.

The liberal arts already teach the skills agents demand. Working well with an agent is mostly an exercise in writing and judgment: stating a problem precisely, breaking it into steps, reading someone else’s work critically and defending a decision. Those are the habits a liberal arts education claims to build in every major. A clear specification is a piece of writing. A code review is an argument with evidence.

Ethics is not a separate course. Agents raise questions students will face on the job: who is responsible for code nobody typed, when and how to disclose AI use, which data should never be pasted into a third-party tool. Small programs can work these questions into every course instead of leaving them to a single ethics requirement.

Undergraduate research can be more ambitious. With agents, a small team of undergraduates can build systems that would have been out of reach a few years ago. That raises the bar for what students need to manage: specifications, branches, code review, tests and continuous integration. In my lab, ADAL, the list of what we look for in student researchers now starts with agentic coding and verifying what agents write, ahead of fluency in any particular language.

The constraints are real. Small colleges do not have rooms full of teaching assistants, every new form of assessment costs faculty time, and agent access costs money. Brown gave the students in its Agentic Studio course $20-a-month Claude plans by design, and the instructors note that those limits “curtailed some of what we asked them to do.” If access depends on what each student can afford, these tools will widen exactly the gaps small colleges work hard to close. Colleges should plan to provide access rather than leave it to individual students.

How I think we should teach with agents

These are the principles I am planning around. None is fully proven, but all are consistent with the evidence above.

  1. Fundamentals by hand first, agents later. Writing code by hand is how students build mental models of how programs work, and the evidence says novices pay the highest price for handing that work off. Introductory courses should keep substantial hand-written work and in-person exams. Brown’s pilot intro course allows only chat tools for the first two months and introduces agents in the last month. Upper-level courses and capstones are where agents belong, used fully.

  2. Grade understanding, not just the artifact. If an agent can produce the artifact, the artifact alone tells me little about what the student learned. Short code walkthroughs, in-class problems and “change this function while I watch” questions show what a student actually understands. In the Utah State course, exam scores held steady, even rising slightly (though not significantly), while the share of pasted code went up.

  3. Make verification a core skill. Treat everything an agent writes as a draft. Students should write tests before asking an agent for code, read every diff, and be able to explain why the result is correct. The Anthropic study found the largest losses in debugging, which is exactly the skill needed to catch an agent’s mistakes. Debugging deserves more class time, not less.

  4. Turn specifications and design into writing assignments. Have students write the specification, the design rationale and the code review, and grade them as seriously as the code. This plays directly to a liberal arts college’s strengths.

  5. Go bigger, earlier. Agents make it realistic for students to work on larger, longer-lived projects much sooner. Use that to teach what employers now look for in new graduates: working in an existing codebase, Git workflows, code review and testing. Brown’s students “found significant value in the peer-review and crit activities.”

  6. Ask for transparency. Brown’s Agentic Studio required reflection journals and chat transcripts. In the instructors’ early observations, most students “developed their own personal boundaries for when to use agents and for how much.” Asking students to show how they worked, not just what they produced, turns reflection into a habit.

The case for the liberal arts gets stronger

Brown’s students named the risk themselves. According to the instructors, “a majority of students were concerned about their lack of understanding of their code bases,” and most worried about the loss of learning if agents arrived in intro courses. That worry is healthy. The goal is not to shield students from these tools, or to hand the tools over without a plan. It is to graduate people who can decide what software should exist, direct agents to build it, and show that it works.

That has always been the promise of a liberal arts education: think clearly, write precisely, weigh evidence and take responsibility for your work. As coding agents take over more of the typing, those skills are no longer the soft side of a computer science degree. They are the job.

If you teach computing at a small college and are trying any of this, I would like to compare notes. You can reach me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • Prather et al., The Widening Gap: The Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers (2024).
  • Shen and Tamkin, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills, Anthropic (January 2026).
  • Becker et al., Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, METR (2025).
  • Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, and the monthly dashboard.
  • Gordon et al., ACM Task Force on Generative AI and Programming Assessment: Final Report (February 2026).
  • Fowles et al., Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom (preprint, May 2026).
  • Brown University, Brown professors devise course to explore generative AI in computer science education (June 2026); Agentic Studio notes for visitors; and CSCI 0111E course design (Fall 2026).
